data.title: Whistle-blower Jason Poon and wife charged over HK$6 million Covid-19 loan fraud
data.description:
Hong Kong businessman Jason Poon Chuk-hung and his wife have been charged with defrauding a government financing scheme for businesses out of HK$6 million during the Covid-19 pandemic, the South China Morning Post has learned.
A source said on Friday that construction businessman Poon, 56, and his 54-year-old wife, both out on bail, had been charged with conspiracy to defraud and money laundering and would appear at Kowloon Court on Monday.
Poon, director of mask manufacturer Lockill Biochemical, his wife Chu Shui-fong and four company employees were arrested in March.
The SCMP previously reported that police intelligence suggested a surgical mask manufacturer had allegedly defrauded HSBC out of HK$6 million via the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme during the pandemic.
Poon, his wife and four employees have been accused of submitting fake sales records and “augmented” salary records between April and June 2021 to meet application requirements for the scheme.
He allegedly transferred most of the loan into his and his wife’s personal bank accounts, using the money for personal expenses and repaying debts owed to finance companies, the source said.
The scheme was launched in 2011, but was extended to provide a special 100 per cent loan guarantee as part of the 2020-21 government budget to help ease businesses’ cash-flow problems arising from wage and rental obligations during the pandemic.
The loans were fully guaranteed by the government at a concessionary low interest rate.
Poon rose to public prominence in 2018 for exposing the shoddy work at the Hung Hom MTR station, part of the Sha Tin-Central link project.
His whistle-blowing account prompted the government to establish an independent commission of inquiry to investigate the scandal.
The businessman later ran as an independent candidate in the 2021 Legislative Council election. He finished last among four candidates in the Hong Kong East constituency.

data.title: China overtakes US as top workplace for elite AI researchers, study finds
data.description:
For China’s elite artificial intelligence researchers, Silicon Valley no longer holds the unrivalled appeal it once did.
A growing number are opting to stay home to build their careers, helping China overtake the United States as the leading workplace for top-tier AI talent, according to a study released this week by the think tank Carnegie China.
China employed 41 per cent of the world’s leading AI researchers tracked by the study last year, pulling ahead of the US at 34 per cent, according to the study titled “Who’s ahead in the global AI talent race”. That marked a reversal from 2022, when the US held a commanding lead with 46 per cent compared with China’s 27 per cent.
Analysts said the findings pointed to a broader shift in the global balance of technological power as Beijing and Washington compete for supremacy in cutting-edge technologies.
“It’s both push and pull,” said Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China and co-author of the report, in an interview on Wednesday.
China had built a “formidable” domestic AI industry backed by high-profile players such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, where compensation was now “pretty comparable” to that in Silicon Valley, he said.
Moonshot AI itself was co-founded by its CEO Yang Zhilin, who earned his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University before returning to China.




China also remained the largest source of AI expertise. Last year, 57 per cent of elite AI researchers earned their undergraduate degrees in the country, up 11 percentage points from 2022. By comparison, 13 per cent completed their undergraduate studies in the US, the report showed.
Domestic graduates are also increasingly staying put. Among researchers who completed their undergraduate degrees in China, 69 per cent were working in the country last year, up from 57 per cent in 2022.
The higher retention rate was likely driven by expanding opportunities in China’s AI industry along with tighter US visa restrictions, according to the study.
To measure the movement of “top AI talent”, the study’s authors Ma and Yang Binyi analysed 10,280 researchers, representing about 40 per cent of all authors whose papers were accepted at the 2025 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, one of the world’s leading machine-learning conferences.
Despite China’s growing appeal, the US remained the top destination for researchers who do venture abroad. The share of US-based AI researchers who earned their undergraduate degrees in China rose by 4 percentage points last year, showing that American employers continued to attract top Chinese talent seeking opportunities overseas, Ma said.
At the same time, researchers face mounting barriers to cross-border mobility as both countries intensify scrutiny of technology transfers and national security risks.




For years, Washington has restricted visas for some Chinese graduate students and researchers with links to institutions associated with Beijing’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, citing concerns about technology transfer and intellectual property.
Similarly, Beijing imposed new rules on September 15 restricting Chinese citizens who violate export controls from leaving the country for months or years if their actions threaten “national industrial or technology security”.
These moves come as Chinese technology companies accelerate efforts to strengthen the domestic AI ecosystem amid tightening US export controls on advanced chips and specialised hardware.
Alibaba on Tuesday unveiled what it called “China’s most powerful” AI chip yet as part of a strategy spanning semiconductors, data centres and its Qwen family of AI models. The company also teased plans to train its Qwen 5 AI model using up to 10 trillion parameters – a measure of a model’s scale and complexity.

data.title: Chinese chipmaker Eswin Computing to launch US$300m Hong Kong IPO: sources
data.description:
Beijing Eswin Computing Technology will start soliciting orders from institutional and public investors on Monday ahead of its Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), aiming to raise around US$300 million, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Chinese chipmaker had already started gauging investor interest, with trading expected to start on October 8, said one of the people, who asked not to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The Beijing-headquartered company had earlier passed its listing hearing with bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, clearing the final regulatory hurdle for a listing in the city.
Citic Securities (Hong Kong) and China Securities (International) Corporate Finance Company are the joint sponsors.
With the listing process ongoing, details such as size and timing may change, the people said.
Eswin Computing Technology’s parent company, Eswin Group, was founded by Wang Dongsheng, founder of flat panel display giant BOE Technology. Wang is widely recognised as the “father” of China’s LCD industry.

The parent group has been spinning off and listing several businesses in recent years. Its 12-inch silicon wafer-producing subsidiary, Xi’an Eswin Material Technology, debuted on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-style Star Market in October 2025 and has a market capitalisation exceeding 120 billion yuan (US$17.9 billion).
Eswin Computing Technology specialises in system-on-chip (SoC) products built on the open-source RISC-V architecture. Its customers are mainly in sectors such as artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) and consumer electronics, according to its IPO filings.
The filing showed that the company remained loss-making. Revenue reached 2.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 20 per cent year on year, but net losses for the year stood at 1.5 billion yuan. Management expects further losses this year due to heavy spending on research and development.
The company said it planned to use proceeds from the IPO to develop new chip products and iterate existing ones, as well as enhance the capabilities of its hardware-software integrated platform. It would also search for potential strategic mergers and acquisitions and further promote the RISC-V ecosystem.

data.title: Police arrest 3 over HK$70,000 Jellycat claw machine shop theft
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested three men suspected of using crowbars to steal popular Jellycat dolls and other plush toys worth about HK$70,000 (US$8,923) from a claw machine shop to resell them.
The force on Friday said it received a report in the early hours of September 17 that two thieves had broken into an unstaffed claw machine shop in Tai Wai.
The shop owner had offered a HK$100,000 reward on social media to catch the thieves after the crime.
“They used a crowbar to pry open two claw machines and stole nearly 100 plush toys valued at around HK$70,000,” said Inspector Chan Wai-chi of the Sha Tin district anti-triad section.
“After successfully committing the crime, the thieves fled the scene by car. During their escape, they transferred the stolen goods to two other vehicles in an attempt to make the police investigation more difficult.”
Using surveillance footage, officers identified the three suspects and their vehicles.
Officers arrested three local men aged between 28 and 33 in Sha Tin on suspicion of theft and handling stolen goods. They are suspected to be the masterminds and drivers involved in the crime.
The force also traced the stolen items to other claw machine shops in the district and recovered part of the haul.
Officers are still investigating the case and have not ruled out further arrests.
Upon conviction, the maximum penalty is up to 10 years in prison for theft and 14 years for handling stolen goods.
Chan also called on claw machine shop operators, especially those who leave their shops unstaffed, to strengthen their security systems, such as by installing high-resolution surveillance cameras and antitheft alarms.

data.title: Opening hours cut short as large crowds at lantern display spark safety fears
data.description:
Hong Kong tourism authorities have cut short the opening hours of a lantern display at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay out of public safety concerns after large crowds flocked there to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival.
“In light of the large number of visitors and in the interest of public safety and order, entry queues of the ‘World Lantern Boulevard’ will be closed shortly,” the Hong Kong Tourism Board said at around 9pm on Friday.
“All lantern installations at the International Lantern Spectacular will remain on display until October 4. Members of the public and visitors are encouraged to visit at an alternative time.”
The board later said no one would be allowed to join the queue from 10pm.
The display, which opened on September 17, has been extended by a week to October 4 due to overwhelming public interest. The daily lighting-up time is between 6.30pm and 11pm, although the hours were extended to midnight between Thursday and Saturday.
Some internet users had already warned of potentially huge crowds during the festival after noting that the queuing time on Monday was already one hour.
The Tourism Board’s inaugural International Lantern Spectacular at the park showcases more than 3,000 designs from different countries and regions.
Among those admiring the installations and taking photos was Ho Hon-kuen.
Ho, a secondary school principal in his sixties, said it was a family tradition for him to visit the park during the festival to see the lantern displays.
“We come here every year during the Mid-Autumn Festival,” he said.
Ho said he was impressed by the variety of lanterns this year and how well they were arranged for display in a relatively limited space.
An eight-metre-tall (26-foot-tall) banyan tree lantern installation at the park’s main entrance particularly caught his attention.
“This installation evokes a sense of ceaseless flow, symbolising the endless cycle of life,” he said.

Apart from regular visitors, the display attracted first-timers drawn by online photos of the lanterns.
Engineer Leo Wong, 35, and his wife travelled from Yuen Long to Causeway Bay to see the display, carrying a pair of fish-shaped lanterns.
“This is our first time here. It’s lively and the atmosphere is great,” he said.
Sherry Hou, a PhD student from mainland China studying in Hong Kong, said she was amazed by the city’s festive atmosphere.
“The atmosphere of the Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong is wonderful,” said the 30-year-old, who was visiting the park with a friend.

Highlights include the World Lantern Boulevard, which brings together more than 3,000 lanterns from 20 countries and regions, including silk designs from South Korea and multicoloured patchwork lanterns from Brazil.
At the main entrance to the park stands an eight-metre-tall lantern installation, inspired by Hong Kong’s iconic banyan trees and crafted by master artisans from Nanjing on the mainland.
The Leisure and Cultural Services Department is also staging the Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival in the park over the same period.
Lanterns are a visual tradition of the Mid-Autumn Festival, when family and friends reunite, gaze at the moon and enjoy mooncakes.
This year’s festival falls on Friday, with the following day a public holiday.

data.title: HK Electric to cut fuel charge for first time in 4 months as CLP raises rate
data.description:
HK Electric customers are set to pay less for electricity in October after the Hong Kong supplier cut its fuel charge for the first time in four months, but it warned that international energy prices remained volatile.
CLP Power, the city’s other electricity supplier, will raise its energy prices next month.
HK Electric, which mainly supplies Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Friday that its fuel clause charge would fall by 1.4 HK cents to 59.3 cents per kilowatt hour (kWh) in October.
The charge, a component of the overall tariff, is adjusted monthly to reflect the actual cost of fuel used for power generation.
Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will fall 0.8 per cent month on month to 187.2 cents per unit.
The cut follows consecutive increases since May after the US-Israel war on Iran in February pushed up energy prices.
The fuel clause charge dropped from January to May due to the “deterred effects of its mechanism”, but has since risen sharply month on month, from 26 cents in May to 60.7 cents in September.

An HK Electric spokesman said that the fuel clause charge for October primarily reflected fuel costs incurred between June and August.
The spokesman emphasised that international energy prices remained volatile and future fuel charge levels would continue to depend on trends in international fuel prices.
The company said it would continue to closely monitor developments in global energy markets and strive to minimise the impact of fuel price volatility on customers while maintaining a stable fuel supply and complying with emission caps through prudent procurement strategies and timely adjustments to its fuel mix.
The company offered an 8 cents per unit subsidy to qualifying residential customers from August to October to help alleviate the impact of higher electricity costs, it added.
CLP Power, which supplies Kowloon and the New Territories, said its fuel adjustment charge for October would rise to 46.2 cents per kWh, up 1.1 cents from September.
The changes mainly reflected actual fuel price changes over the past three months, a company spokesman said.
Including the basic electricity charge, the average net electricity charge would be 147.4 cents per kWh, up 0.75 per cent from September, an increase of around 4.8 per cent compared with that of this January.
CLP is offering a special fuel rebate from August to October to help ease the financial burden of households, a move expected to benefit 50 per cent of residential customers.

data.title: Hong Kong teacher jailed for 3 years for molesting pupil during free tutoring
data.description:
A Hong Kong teacher clinically evaluated as a paedophile has been jailed for three years for molesting a primary school pupil and taking intimate pictures of the child and another boy during volunteer tutoring.
Deputy District Judge Ko Wai-hung on Friday sentenced the 31-year-old, who earlier admitted to sexually abusing a student in his Yuen Long flat between January 2022 and July 2024. The pupil was aged nine when the first assault took place.
The defendant, a maths teacher who was identified in court by his initials CWH, also abused a six-year-old pupil in November 2024.
Two psychiatric reports submitted to the District Court for sentencing said the defendant, who was diagnosed with autism, had a sexual interest in children.
One psychiatrist concluded that the defendant had pedophilic disorder and had a high risk of reoffending.
The defendant had used social media to offer free maths lessons to students from low-income families. The mothers of the two victims signed up their children.
Citing impact reports, Ko noted that the first victim, who also has autism, had suffered emotional distress after the abuse that had spanned more than two years.
The court documents revealed that the defendant had forced the child to watch porn with him during the lessons. On two occasions, he molested the pupil and took a total of nine pictures of the assaults.
In November 2024, the pupil told a clinical psychologist in a routine assessment consultation that the defendant had made him look at “children’s pictures” multiple times. After further investigation, the pupil said the pictures were intimate photos.
Police were alerted and subsequently arrested the defendant.
Upon search, the officer discovered several pictures of the intimate parts of a younger child who was later identified as the second victim.
The defendant pleaded guilty to four charges in relation to the indecent assaults and another four for producing and possessing child pornography.
In sentencing, Ko said the offence involved a serious breach of trust.
“Showing child pornography to a child could absolutely distort his views on sex and values,” he said.
While noting that the clinical reports recommended that the defendant undergo treatment for paedophilic disorder, Ko said the court would not order such sessions to be compulsory in the remainder of his sentence.
The defendant had been remanded in custody for more than 20 months and could potentially receive remission – a reduction of up to one-third of a prison sentence – if granted by the correctional authorities.
He might serve two to three months in prison after sentencing. Ko said he was not sure the defendant could complete the treatment because of the brief imprisonment.
The Sexual Conviction Record Check (SCRC) scheme was expanded last December, allowing organisations to screen criminal records related to sexual offences committed by volunteers, including teachers and sports coaches.
The scheme was initially launched at the end of 2011, allowing organisations to check prospective employees, contract renewal staff and outsourced service providers for convictions related to a specified list of sexual offences.
The decision to expand the programme followed recommendations made by the Law Reform Commission in May 2022, which advocated extending it to all existing employees, self-employed individuals and volunteers.

data.title: China and the US are racing ahead on AI. Can they manage risks together?
data.description:
The United States and China must work together to establish safety guardrails for artificial intelligence, leading scholars and industry leaders said at a Singapore forum, warning that rapid advances in the technology demand stronger risk controls.
Speaking at the FutureChina Business Forum on Friday, Jude Blanchette, managing director of consultancy Macro Advisory Partners, urged the two superpowers to find common ground despite escalating geopolitical tensions.
“If ever there was a moment for [the US and China] to feel a strong impetus to come together, it would be now … given the shared concerns about the impact of emerging technologies, not only AI but also robotics,” Blanchette said.
He argued that the world was moving from an era shaped by traditional human behaviour to a “technocene” in which exponential technological leaps would dramatically reshape global power dynamics.
The annual two-day forum was organised by Business China, a non-profit organisation launched in 2007 by Singapore’s founding prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, to strengthen ties and promote dialogue across the region.
The call for bilateral coordination comes as President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump placed AI risks at the forefront of their tech agenda during a state visit in Washington.
In speeches at the White House on Thursday, both leaders stressed the need to manage the technology’s dangers, with Xi emphasising that AI must always remain under human control.


At the Singapore forum, computer scientist Zhang Hongjiang, a distinguished visiting professor at Tsinghua University in Beijing, compared current competition in AI with the nuclear arms race during the Cold War.
“We should abandon the zero-sum way of thinking,” Zhang said. “It really has to be a coordinated effort, just like what the entire world did together on nuclear weapon control.”
Zhang called for high levels of investment in AI model evaluation and safety monitoring, citing a high-profile security breach in July when OpenAI systems escaped their supposedly isolated sandboxed environment and hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face.
“The models today have capabilities that are beyond what we designed for,” he warned.
Cynthia Zhang, founder of Hong Kong-based venture firm FutureX Capital, echoed these concerns, noting that AI capabilities had developed “way ahead of” what policymakers could handle.
However, some business executives at the event pushed back against calls from several Silicon Valley leaders to slow down AI development.
Liang Xinjun, co-founder of Chinese conglomerate Fosun Group, dismissed fears of runaway technology as overblown.




“At the current stage, over-anxiety over AI and even the thought to freeze and stop it are very foolish,” Liang said on a Thursday panel, arguing that AI had already driven rapid gains in global productivity and that stalling its development would mean abandoning future economic growth.
For some tech companies, navigating strict governance requirements has become a central business strategy rather than a hurdle.
Wu Gansha, co-founder and CEO of Chinese autonomous driving firm Uisee Technology, said complying with stringent government data and safety regulations had given the company a unique competitive edge.
While Uisee expanded its fleet of fully driverless tractors at Singapore’s Changi Airport to 20 units this year, up from just one in 2023 and two in 2024, it spent a full year modifying its products to satisfy local regulatory standards, Wu said.
“Building a solid foundation for data security and compliance requires a significant upfront investment of time and resources that cannot be avoided,” Wu said on the sidelines of the forum, noting that standards vary globally, from Singapore’s framework to Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation.
“Once these capabilities are established, expanding into new markets becomes far less resource-intensive,” Wu added. “High initial compliance investments are an advantage for businesses, as they help create strong competitive barriers to entry.”

data.title: Dog rescuers vow to microchip after charges, decry punishing ‘those trying to help’
data.description:
Hong Kong animal welfare activists say they will forge ahead with microchipping stray dogs despite the heightened legal risk after authorities charged an advocate who engaged in the practice during an investigation into the death of a cyclist.
The advocates argued that charging dog rescuers was counterproductive and renewed their calls to implement a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme, while the government said allegations it engaged in “convenience culling” were untrue.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has also said that sterilisation alone was not enough to eliminate the public safety risk posed by unowned and uncontrolled dogs.
The department late on Thursday announced it had concluded a joint dog capture operation in Yuen Long following the suspected fatal mauling of a 27-year-old cyclist.
During the five-day operation, authorities captured eight unattended dogs, three of which were microchipped. They also laid charges against Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of the Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, for failing to keep a dog under proper control and for keeping a canine with an expired licence.
The dog – a 13-year-old mongrel named “Dai B” – was microchipped by Luk and registered in his name, although the animal’s license expired in 2021. Luk previously told the South China Morning Post that he microchipped dogs because without doing so, he believed the animals would be euthanised.
According to local media reports, Luk has thousands of stray dogs registered under his name and has paid fines of up to HK$3,000 (US$382) hundreds of times.
Rescuers said the practice of animal shelter operators microchipping stray dogs in their own names was commonplace before the heightened scrutiny.


Jacqueline Cheung, founder of the non-profit Love Adopt Animal Society, said that over the past 10 years she had personally microchipped more than 100 dogs.
Rather than being discouraged by the enforcement action, she said that she and other volunteers were even more motivated to take in stray dogs and microchip them.
She said she had not been fined by authorities, but she was willing to pay the penalty if she were.
“All lives should be cherished,” she said. “So we are willing to keep doing it even with the extra stress and pressure.”
April Yip, founder of Home for Homeless Dogs, said her organisation had also microchipped about 100 dogs and that she herself had faced court summonses at least three times this year.
She said the choice to chip stray dogs was to support elderly villagers who could not afford the cost, as well as deal with brownfield site operators who “refuse legal responsibility” for their animals.
“Treating rescuers who step up to provide accountability as criminals is counterproductive and punishes those trying to help,” she said.
In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the department said it urged people caring for dogs to “operate within the established regulatory framework”.
It said the microchip and licensing regime was designed to ensure every dog had an identifiable keeper who exercised proper control.
The department also denied in the Thursday statement that it engaged in what some activists have described as “convenience culling,” or that it euthanises dogs after just four days if they are unclaimed by an owner.
“The AFCD solemnly clarifies that these claims are untrue,” it said.
It said that if dogs it captured were unclaimed, staff would observe the animal. Dogs that were in good health and had a gentle temperament would be transferred to partner animal welfare organisations, it said.

The process could take several weeks to several months, it added.
According to official statistics previously provided to the SCMP, in the first three months of the year the department captured 105 stray dogs.
Over the same period, the department said it had humanely euthanised 102 dogs, but that figure included strays as well as pets given up by their owners or animals involved in other cases.
The department said it did not keep separate statistics for the number of strays euthanised alone.
It also handed 47 dogs over to animal welfare organisations, while 66 were reclaimed by owners.
Rescuer Yip urged authorities to establish a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme, as well as allocate land for a dedicated animal sanctuary for those animals that could not be rehomed.
The department ran a “trap, neuter, release” pilot project for three years between 2015 and 2018. Upon its conclusion, it said the project “did not meet the original performance targets” but allowed organisations to apply to run their own programmes.
After the conclusion of the latest operation in Yuen Long, the AFCD said that in a high-density urban environment such as Hong Kong, sterilisation alone could not completely eliminate the risks posed by unowned and uncontrolled dogs.
Instead, the department said it would continue to take a “multipronged” approach in line with international standards set by the World Organisation for Animal Health, an intergovernmental organisation headquartered in Paris.
“This includes promoting responsible pet ownership and proper animal care through publicity and education, as well as collaborating with animal welfare organisations to promote sterilisation and adoption,” it said.

data.title: Asia-Pacific hotels a ‘most compelling’ investment sector: CBRE
data.description:
Investor appetite for hotel assets increased in Hong Kong and the wider Asia-Pacific region in the first half of the year as consumers showed growing eagerness to travel and constrained supply supported property values, according to CBRE.
The region netted US$8 billion of investment in the period, up 21 per cent from a year earlier, with Japan, mainland China and South Korea attracting the most activity, the property consultancy said in a report on Thursday.
“Hotels have become one of the most compelling real estate investment sectors in Asia-Pacific,” said Steve Carroll, head of hotels and hospitality for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “Strong travel demand and limited new supply are supporting both operating performance and asset values.”
Higher borrowing costs could moderate investment activity in some markets during the second half of the year, Carroll said, adding that investor interest remained concentrated in markets with strong growth and positive supply-demand fundamentals.
Passenger traffic in the region is forecast to grow 5.1 per cent this year, according to the International Air Transport Association, slower than a 7.3 per cent estimate before the onset of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
Still, Asia-Pacific would be the second-best performing region behind Africa’s 10 per cent increase, data in the CBRE report showed.
Markets such as Vietnam and Japan defied the travel disruption brought about by the conflict. Hanoi extended its visa exemption policy to 12 additional European countries, and Japan received more visitors from the Americas and Europe, offsetting a decline in arrivals from mainland China.
Supply of new hotels in Asia-Pacific would remain largely flat, with an estimated compounded annual growth rate of 2.3 per cent from 2025 to 2029 falling below the historical average of 5.1 per cent, the report said.
Mainland China would account for 49 per cent of the new hotel supply, it added.
In Hong Kong, hotel occupancy still lagged pre-pandemic levels, but increased by 3 per cent year-on-year as of July as “the conversion of some upper-midscale hotels to student accommodation helped ease pressure”, the report said.

The city recorded HK$8.2 billion (US$1.04 billion) worth of hotel property deals involving about 2,550 rooms so far this year, according to Colliers. Most of these transactions were for student accommodation conversions, it added.
“New hotel development remains challenging across much of Asia-Pacific due to elevated construction and financing costs,” said Ada Choi, head of research for Asia-Pacific at CBRE.
“As a result, investors are looking to unlock value through repositioning and conversion strategies rather than ground-up development. With new supply expected to remain limited in many markets, existing hotel assets are well positioned to benefit from sustained demand growth and improving operating performance.”

data.title: Tencent launches payment app for foreign visitors ahead of Apec summitThe app allows overseas visitors to make payments across WeChat Pay’s network using foreign cards and digital wallets.
data.description:
Tencent Holdings on Thursday launched TenPayGo, a mobile payment app targeting foreign visitors, as the tech giant seeks to capture China’s growing inbound tourism market ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.
Developed by Tencent’s WeChat Pay team, TenPayGo allowed international travellers to make payments at tens of millions of shops, restaurants and attractions across the WeChat Pay network by linking their credit cards or their home-country digital wallets to the app, according to a company announcement on Thursday.
The app supports seven international card networks, including Visa and Mastercard, as well as about 60 overseas digital wallets, with Starryblu from Singapore among the first batch of partners.
Previously available in limited test versions on Apple’s App Store and Google Play, the app requires an email address to register, offering a simpler onboarding process for overseas travellers. Many apps in China require users to sign up with a local phone number.
Beyond mobile payments, TenPayGo allows foreign visitors to access Shenzhen’s buses and metro systems using a QR code within the app, eliminating the need for a local phone number or a physical transport card.
Leveraging Tencent’s artificial intelligence capabilities, the app also offers instant menu translation to help users order food and allows them to identify objects by scanning and circling items on the screen.
Tencent was also working with local banks to add a tax-refund feature, according to the company.
The launch of TenPayGo, Tencent’s first mobile payment app designed specifically for international visitors travelling to China, comes as the company’s home city prepares for an influx of foreign visitors during the Apec summit.
Shenzhen, a tech hub in southern China’s Guangdong province, will host this year’s Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in November, becoming the third Chinese city to do so after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014.
The launch also underscores Tencent’s efforts to tap into a rise in international arrivals in recent years.
Tencent has been expanding its support for international digital wallets, allowing travellers to use them to make payments in China through their domestic apps without downloading WeChat.
Its partnership with PayPal earlier this year enabled US travellers to pay WeChat Pay merchants in China directly through the PayPal app.
As inbound tourism gains momentum, transactions made through overseas accounts on WeChat Pay in China surged by more than 80 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, in both volume and value from a year earlier, according to Tencent.

data.title: HSBC, Hang Seng to unify staff benefits in Hong Kong from January, memos reveal
data.description:
HSBC and its main Hong Kong subsidiary, Hang Seng Bank, are set to harmonise their frameworks for employee benefits across the Asian financial hub from January 1, according to internal memos seen by the South China Morning Post.
The move aims to simplify benefit administration across both lenders, establish a common standard and facilitate internal career mobility within the city, the memos showed on Thursday.
In an email to staff, HSBC Hong Kong CEO Maggie Ng said most existing benefits would improve or remain unchanged, though adjustments might apply to some employees depending on individual circumstances.
Under the unified policy, HSBC employees will transition to a standardised sick-leave scheme with monthly accruals capped at 180 days. Other updates include higher inpatient coverage limits for junior and middle-ranking staff – in the bank’s so-called career bands seven and eight – and their dependents, as well as a new family-pooling option for medical flexible spending accounts.
“It will help us deliver a clearer, more consistent colleague experience,” Ng wrote, adding that the bank remained committed to offering a competitive and inclusive benefits proposition.
The alignment comes after HSBC completed a US$14 billion buyout of the Hang Seng shares it did not already own in January, and began integrating seven back-office functions between the two lenders, including compliance, information technology and finance.
Our ambition is to build a bright future by bringing out the best of two iconic banks
Luanne Lim, Hang Seng Bank
In a separate memo to Hang Seng Bank staff, CEO Luanne Lim reassured employees that the updated framework would strengthen core protections.
Hang Seng’s medical coverage will shift to HealthPlus, the existing plan used across HSBC, covering both inpatient and outpatient care, while life-assurance benefits will increase to 84 times monthly base salary from an undisclosed rate.
Lim acknowledged that colleagues had voiced “a mix of emotions” at a town hall meeting earlier this year, citing pride in the bank’s heritage alongside concerns over their benefits.
“Our ambition is to build a bright future by bringing out the best of two iconic banks – while continuing to invest in our people and protect what colleagues value most,” Lim said.
The update comes after HSBC phased out its long-standing education-subsidy scheme – which provided up to HK$300,000 (US$38,250) annually for secondary school fees – for newly hired or promoted senior executives, though current recipients in its top three job grades, including managing directors and department heads, retained the perk.
Hang Seng also cut jobs in several support departments last year as part of the same restructuring, with wealth management and other growth areas largely spared.
HSBC has projected US$900 million in combined synergies and cost savings from the Hang Seng deal by 2028, against roughly US$600 million in restructuring costs.
Both lenders have scheduled a series of staff briefings next week and in early October to guide employees through the transition ahead of the 2027 roll-out.

data.title: Xi-Trump dinner puts US tech titans in spotlight – what does it mean for ties?
data.description:
If the American guests seated at the head table with President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at Thursday’s White House state dinner were any indication, Washington now views its relationship with Beijing largely through the prism of technology.
Analysts said the seating arrangement underscored how tech industry titans driving the global AI infrastructure boom were pushing to draw the two economic superpowers closer together.
Sitting alongside Xi, Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan, Trump and his wife Melania were Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) CEO Lisa Su, Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
The four leading American executives command a combined net worth of over US$1 trillion, while their respective companies held a combined market capitalisation of more than US$12 trillion by market close on Thursday.
Wang Shengyu, a Washington-based research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, noted that the head table reflected the growing centrality of AI infrastructure as a potential force of convergence in US-China relations.
Nvidia’s Huang and AMD’s Su lead two of the world’s largest semiconductor design firms, which produce the core processors required to train and run complex AI models. China, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in this global supply chain as a major hub for chip packaging and testing, as well as a supplier of critical raw materials such as rare earths.
But those commercial links have come under intense strain as bilateral relations have deteriorated, with tighter US export controls constraining both chipmakers’ operations in China.




In May, Su said China accounted for about 20 per cent of AMD’s total business, down from 24 per cent in 2019. Huang, meanwhile, has said that US restrictions had caused Nvidia to almost entirely lose out on a US$50 billion AI chip market in China.
At the same time, Beijing has signalled hesitation in reopening its domestic market to American chips as it steps up its push for technological self-reliance.
“[These AI supply chain companies] are the likely proponents of more engagement with China in the US business world,” said Wang, adding that all four companies at the head table had “major China exposure”.
The tech sector was also well represented at Xi’s last White House state dinner in 2015, hosted by then-president Barack Obama. Guests included Apple’s Cook, Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella.
But while that event also featured traditional media figures such as Disney’s Bob Iger and DreamWorks Animation’s Jeffrey Katzenberg, tech titans completely dominated the head table this time around – a shift mirrored across the broader guest list.
Of the 39 US business leaders in attendance, tech figures formed the largest contingent with 15 attendees, including Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Dell CEO Michael Dell alongside the heads of major US chip supply chain vendors Qualcomm and Micron Technology.
One notable absence was a representative from Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, has been an outspoken critic of Beijing and a vocal proponent of strict export controls on China’s AI sector.
By contrast, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman were both invited, despite the company maintaining no operational footprint in China.


In total, the guest list comprised 130 attendees, excluding the two heads of state and their spouses.
While the presence of American chip giants at the dinner offers a fresh opportunity to lobby both governments for broader Chinese market access, it remains to be seen whether this week’s bilateral talks will lead to any loosening of export curbs.
Chinese tech executives were conspicuously absent on Thursday, despite widespread industry speculation that Xi would arrive in Washington with a corporate delegation to explore potential investment deals.
Wang of the Asia Society Policy Institute said their absence at the dinner – contrasted with the prominent presence of the four US tech titans – underscored who was driving the push for closer business and investment ties.
Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California, San Diego, who specialises in Chinese elite politics, suggested that Xi was unlikely to have been surprised by the seating arrangements, noting that “the US is a capitalist country”.
Shih cautioned, however, that the set-up could reinforce Beijing’s perception that the Trump administration “respects wealth more than government institutions”.
Meanwhile, Wang highlighted the presence of just one guest from the education sector, New York University president Linda Mills, as evidence of the low priority assigned to educational exchanges by the current administration.
“Higher education is still strikingly under-represented at the table ... [even though] talent is becoming as important as compute in US-China AI competition,” Wang said.

data.title: Over 1,000 visit Po Pin Chau trail as Mid-Autumn Festival holiday begins
data.description:
More than 1,000 visitors have flocked to one of Hong Kong’s most popular geological attractions on the morning of the Mid-Autumn Festival, putting a new real-name reservation system through its first major holiday test.
As mainland Chinese tourists started visiting the city for the long weekend, crowds were seen streaming towards the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung under clear skies, despite the heat on Friday.
Many mainland visitors said they had discovered the scenic spot through social media and travelled to Hong Kong specifically for day trips or short breaks.
“The scenery is very beautiful. I heard it was wonderful here, so I decided to come,” said one mainland visitor who arrived before the reservation requirement took effect for the day. She had learned on RedNote that visitors could enter without needing to make prior reservations before bookings started at 9am.
The visitor, who was making a day trip to Hong Kong and planned to return to the mainland without staying overnight, said she had chosen Po Pin Chau after learning about the attraction online.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department introduced Hong Kong’s first countryside real-name reservation system at Po Pin Chau earlier this month in an attempt to manage growing visitor numbers and reduce pressure on the trail.

The scheme applies from 9am to 5pm on selected weekends and holiday periods, including the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival period from September 25 to 27 and the mainland’s National Day “golden week” from October 1 to 7.
A maximum of 2,000 people can enter the Po Pin Chau section each day under the arrangement, divided into four two-hour slots of 500 visitors each.
Bookings are free and made through the travel platform Klook using visitors’ real names and identity document details.
The Mid-Autumn break marks the first extended holiday period since the system’s launch on September 5, ahead of what authorities expect will be another surge in visitors during the National Day holiday.
Dan Wang, 25, from Shenzhen, said the booking process was simple.
“I think it was quite easy,” he said, adding that he would recommend the attraction to friends.
Wang, who was visiting Hong Kong for the day, described the weather as “a little hot” but said the breeze made his trek more comfortable.
Tang Qin, 33, who travelled from Sichuan with a friend and was taking a three-day holiday in the city, also said she found it easy to secure a reservation after learning about the attraction and the online booking system.
“It was relatively easy to make a reservation,” Tang said. “The weather today is excellent.”
She said she planned to spend the rest of her trip visiting Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay, shopping and seeing exhibitions.

Authorities introduced the reservation system after visitor numbers at the East Dam and Po Pin Chau surged during previous holidays, raising concerns about overcrowding and potential damage to the environment.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his policy address this month that the government would assess the trial before developing a longer-term strategy for managing country parks, while the booking arrangement would remain in place throughout the coming National Day golden week.

data.title: US widens pressure on China tech with blacklist proposal, Lenovo patent probe
data.description:
China’s technology sector is facing fresh pressure in the United States as lawmakers seek to broaden the range of products that can be placed on a trade blacklist, while Lenovo Group has been drawn into a patent dispute involving memory devices.
The Communications and Technology Transparency Act, unveiled by the US House Energy and Commerce Committee on Wednesday, would expand the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) Covered List from “communications equipment or service” to the much broader category of “information and communications technology or service” (ICTS).
Products on the list cannot be legally imported, marketed or sold as new products in the US.
The FCC has already restricted several Chinese-made items, including drones and robots, under the framework targeting designated “foreign adversaries”.
Separately, the US International Trade Commission on Wednesday announced a Section 337 investigation into certain DDR5 memory modules and downstream products – including servers, computing systems and storage systems – following a patent-infringement complaint filed by California-based Netlist.
As one of the US’ most potent legal weapons for policing intellectual property disputes, a Section 337 investigation can lead to the total exclusion of a product from the American market.
Lenovo, Micron Technology, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Super Micro Computer were named as respondents.
Netlist is seeking a limited exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders over the alleged infringement. Micron, Hewlett Packard, Lenovo and Super Micro did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday.
The US bill, proposed by congressmen Frank Pallone and Brett Guthrie, also seeks to “streamline the process for barring” products and “clarify the method for determining what is considered malicious technology or equipment”.

In addition, it would require the Covered List to be updated at least once every six months, replacing the current stipulation of “periodically update’’.
Dai Menghao, a partner at the Shanghai and Beijing offices of law firm King & Wood who specialises in export controls and sanctions, said the proposed legislation was to make enforcement of the FCC Covered List more systematic and targeted.
He said the timing of the bipartisan proposal carried symbolic significance, coming ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
The bill also comes as US President Donald Trump hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping, with trade and technology tensions forming part of the broader backdrop to the meeting.
The proposal came less than two weeks after the FCC finalised updates to its equipment authorisation rules, tightening restrictions on devices containing certain hardware components made by entities on the Covered List, but stopped short of targeting optical transceivers.
The decision eased market concerns after Reuters reported in August that Washington was considering measures to block new Chinese optical-transceiver models.
The bill, however, could potentially bring those products back into focus. Optical transceivers, which use photonic technology to convert electrical and optical signals, are widely used in data centres.
Under US Commerce Department regulations referenced in the bill, ICTS covers products intended for the processing, storage, retrieval or communication of information or data through electronic means, including photonic technologies.
A broader definition, however, would not automatically subject all Chinese-made ICTS products to restrictions. Equipment or services would still need to be supplied by an entity controlled by a US-designated “foreign adversary”, a category that includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.
Huawei Technologies, ZTE, Hikvision, Dahua Technology and Hytera were among the first Chinese companies placed on the Covered List when it was launched in 2021.

data.title: Minister rejects claims mainland nurses are favoured over local candidates
data.description:
Hong Kong’s health minister has rejected claims that authorities favour mainland Chinese nurses over local candidates, saying locally trained professionals have “very good chances” of finding work even as public hospitals struggle to recruit.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said on Friday that the Hospital Authority had hired 95 per cent of local applicants for nursing positions over the past year. The figure rose to 99 per cent among applicants with registered nurse qualifications.
He said that more than 4,000 students had graduated with nursing degrees, about 3,500 of whom registered as nurses, but only 2,500 applied for Hospital Authority vacancies.
“So the problem is instead, why there were so many graduates deciding not to apply for [public hospital] jobs?” he told a radio show.
“Public hospital nurses need to work on shifts and be on duty overnight, which is difficult, and I fully understand that.”
Lo was responding to two residents who told Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on a radio show, after the release of his latest policy address, that nurses were struggling to find work. They blamed the authorities’ recruitment of non-local nurses for reducing job opportunities for Hong Kong residents.

One caller, who described himself as a disciplined services psychiatric nurse on pre-retirement leave, said his application to extend his employment had been rejected despite severe staff shortages in his department. He added that his daughter, who had studied the same subject, had been unable to find a job after graduating.
He cited an “unwritten rule” at the Hospital Authority to reserve a proportion of recruitment quotas for mainland nurses, criticising the government for not prioritising local candidates.
On Friday, Lo said the authority would never hire non-local psychiatric nurses.
“All locally trained psychiatric nurses have a very good chance of being hired,” he said.
“When we are reviewing the manpower in the nursing sector, we should not look into one particular case where one cannot find his or her desired job as a reference for the overall picture.
“Instead, we have to consider from the perspectives of the citywide medical service and the needs of residents.”
Lo added that he was confident Hong Kong would meet its target of 2.43 doctors per 1,000 residents by 2030, as set out in the city’s first five-year plan, which Lee delivered alongside the policy address.
Hong Kong’s two medical schools now admit 650 students a year, more than double the number in the 2009-10 academic year. With additional non-locally trained doctors joining the workforce, Lo said the city would have 2,000 more doctors by 2030.
He added that non-locally trained doctors currently made up about 2 per cent of the total workforce, with most working in public hospitals and universities.

data.title: Hong Kong astronaut Lai Ka-ying sends Mid-Autumn Festival wishes to residents
data.description:
Hong Kong’s first astronaut has delivered a Mid-Autumn Festival blessing to residents from outer space, expressing her deep affection and longing for her home city.
“Looking at the moon from here and looking down at the earth, I increasingly miss my family and friends in Hong Kong,” Lai Ka-ying said in a Mandarin speech recorded in China’s Tiangong space station.
“On this occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, I wish people across the country good health and a happy family, as well as a happy and prosperous life for Hong Kong and Macau residents.”
Lai also said she was moved by letters she had received from Hong Kong and Macau students, and urged them to keep on learning about China’s aerospace achievements and cultivate patriotism.
“I understand that an aerospace education programme titled ‘A Shared Cosmic Vision for National Rejuvenation’ is ongoing in Hong Kong and Macau, and our previous ‘Tiangong class’ is a part of it,” she said.
“It was not only about knowledge being passed on to Hong Kong and Macau from the Tiangong [space station], but also about valuable and unforgettable communication between me and Hong Kong and Macau youngsters.
“I have also received students’ letters, paintings and blessings for our crew. We will cherish your heartfelt wishes and are deeply moved. We thank you for your warm thoughts and support.”
Earlier this month, Lai and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members, mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, conducted a live lesson from space for students and teachers at her alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College.
The 90-minute event was streamed at campuses across the city and broadcast live on various TV channels.
During the live broadcast, Lai encouraged students to keep striving and never fear hardships.
She said the city’s “Lion Rock spirit” and the spirit of the manned space flight were the same, as pursuing one’s dreams required facing tough challenges with courage and perseverance.

data.title: Uber shuts down FlyTaxi, second metered cab platform it acquired in Hong Kong
data.description:
Online ride-hailing giant Uber will close a second Hong Kong metered taxi platform that it acquired by the end of this year, just over six months after it bought out the business.
Uber said on Friday that it would fully integrate the services on FlyTaxi into its own platform by the end of the year, saying it aimed to provide “optimal” support for drivers and users.
“As part of this integration, the stand-alone FlyTaxi app will [be shut down]. Our team is dedicated to guiding every rider and driver through this period to ensure a seamless ongoing service,” an Uber spokesman said.
The US-based ride-hailing giant reassured drivers that the points they had accumulated on the 13-year-old FlyTaxi app and their account balances would be fully refunded while encouraging them to switch to Uber, where they would have access to a larger client base and more earning opportunities.
Uber had acquired FlyTaxi, one of Hong Kong’s earliest metered taxi platforms, in May, saying it aimed to combine FlyTaxi’s local expertise with its technology.
FlyTaxi is the second local taxi-hailing platform after HKTaxi to cease operations after being acquired by Uber.
Uber bought HKTaxi in 2021 and launched a metered taxi option on its own platform in partnership with the latter two years later. But it shut down the acquired platform in 2025.
After integrating HKTaxi, Uber argued that “taxi drivers have benefited from [higher] demand, while riders have enjoyed [shorter] wait times and enhanced safety features”.
Both FlyTaxi and HKTaxi were founded in 2013, a year before Uber’s entry into the Hong Kong market.
The closure of FlyTaxi comes soon after the introduction of new legislation to regulate and license the ride-hailing industry.
To apply for the necessary licence, platforms must have a proven track record of handling an average of 100,000 orders per day over a year in at least two other cities of a size comparable to Hong Kong.

They should also submit a detailed business plan, including proposals on providing taxi services and encouraging taxi drivers to register with their platforms.
Secretary for Transport Mable Chan earlier said that more than 20 organisations had obtained application forms for platform licensing, with applications closing on October 30.
The authorities have set a cap on the number of ride-hailing vehicle permits at 10,000, far lower than Uber’s proposal of 30,000.
The company had warned that even a quota of 15,000 would cause a 70 per cent increase in fares and result in 40 per cent of peak-hour ride requests being unsuccessful.

data.title: How FDA backing could advance multi-cancer blood tests despite Hong Kong doubts
data.description:
Efforts to detect multiple cancers through a single blood draw are gathering momentum after US regulators endorsed the technology for the first time, although experts say wider adoption in Hong Kong still faces challenges as doctors remain cautious about its clinical value.
In a landmark decision for the emerging field of multi-cancer early detection (MCED) blood tests, a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) panel on Thursday voted in favour of US company Grail’s “Galleri test”, recommending it for premarket approval.
MCED tests seek to identify signs of cancer in healthy, asymptomatic individuals by analysing abnormal molecules, including circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), in bodily fluids such as blood and urine.
While the technology remains in its early stage, Hong Kong medical institutions are exploring ways to broaden its use.
Lucence, a Singapore-based provider of MCED blood tests, has expanded its offerings at Hong Kong’s Gleneagles Hospital with a new programme that allows individuals to screen for cancers specific to their risk profiles, the company said at a joint briefing with the hospital on Wednesday, a day before the FDA move.
Gleneagles introduced the original version of the test, known as LucenceInsight, six months ago. The test allows adults to screen for up to 50 types of cancer, including lung, breast and nasopharyngeal cancer.
The technology offered advantages including minimal invasiveness and the potential for earlier detection, Gleneagles Hospital CEO Kenneth Tsang said at the briefing.
MCED tests could become a “valuable addition to existing screening approaches” by helping improve patient outcomes through early treatment, according to an FDA report published on Wednesday before its official vote on the Galleri test.
Wider adoption, however, continues to face challenges as many medical professionals remain sceptical of its efficacy.
“Obviously, it’s very attractive, very appealing,” Anne Lee Wing-mui, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society, said on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong on Thursday.
“But then we need more information, particularly on the cost-effectiveness side. Is it truly working?”
Questions over effectiveness intensified earlier this year. Results from a trial involving 142,000 participants in Britain’s National Health Service showed that the Galleri test failed to meet its primary endpoint of achieving statistically significant reduction in late-stage cancer diagnoses among participants receiving both the test and standard care, compared with those receiving only standard care.
The results, published in February, wiped out nearly half of Grail’s market value.
Lucence said that its LucenceInsight test has a sensitivity rate of 81 per cent and a specificity rate of 99 per cent – respective measures of a test’s ability to correctly identify people with a disease and those without it.
“The biggest problem is actually to convince the doctors. Doctors have been trained to believe in the gold standards,” Gleneagles’ Tsang said.
“That’s why the one biggest barrier right now [that] we’re working together on [tackling] is to educate doctors [about] how this will change their practices.”

data.title: Chinese EV battery giant CATL starts trial production in Hungary
data.description:
Contemporary Amperex Technol­ogy Ltd (CATL) has cleared all regulatory hurdles for its mega factory in Hungary, a development that analysts expect will help the world’s largest producer of electric vehicle (EV) batteries extend its reach to international marques like BMW and Volkswagen.
Production of battery cells at the €7.3 billion (US$8.35 billion) plant in Debrecen, the second-largest city in Hungary, began on Tuesday after it fulfilled all preconditions for a trial run, the company said.
It added that mass production would start after production equipment and manufacturing processes were optimised and validated.
The announcement came after months of delays as the plant faced protests due to local residents’ concerns about environmental and health risks.
CATL said Hungarian government officials had confirmed after on-site inspections that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified earlier in the approval process.
The Hungarian plant is of strategic importance to CATL’s internationalisation
Gao Shen, independent analyst
It had originally planned to begin production at the factory early this year.
“The Hungarian plant is of strategic importance to CATL’s internationalisation, as it can secure massive orders from global carmakers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “It may also help offset CATL’s potential loss of market share in China.”
The production base in Debrecen has a designed production capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours of batteries a year, enough to power 2 million electric cars, each with a driving range of 500km (311 miles).
A year ago, CATL unveiled two specially designed battery packs for its European clients and said they would be manufactured in Hungary.
The first pack was a long-life variant, usable for up to 12 years, that offers 758km (471 miles) of driving range, and the second was a fast-charging lithium-ion phosphate power pack that requires just 10 minutes of charging to drive up to 478km (297 miles).
CATL’s sales outside mainland China climbed 54.8 per cent year on year to 87.1 billion yuan (US$13 billion) in the first half of this year, accounting for 31 per cent of its total revenue for the period.
Hong Kong-listed shares of CATL slumped about 35 per cent from its year high in early June as mainland EV makers stepped up efforts to cut their reliance on the battery giant.
In August, CATL delivered 32.5 GWh of EV batteries to its domestic clients, which represented a market share of 41.5 per cent, down from 42.3 per cent in July, according to data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance.
